t97b_parent:
The Parent You Inherited
I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.
If it’s a critic, the parent you inherited also measures whatever you show the world against an impossible ideal, and then attacks you from both sides: you’re not good enough, and anything that does look good is fake anyway. That second one means nothing you do could ever count, and it’s one place feeling fake can come from. When a new grown-up voice shows up saying “Trust me,” of course your little one doesn’t answer.
But with the borrowed adulthood trick, the new grown-up can start outside your head, as someone who likes you the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little one, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. Your little one can watch you do it many times before trusting you, while the parent you inherited calls it fake.
A good routine still feels like lockdown to your little one when it’s run in the warden’s tone. Talking back to the warden can feel disloyal, so I’d give that voice a name of its own, like the Critic. Then start a little rap sheet of its lines, with who used to say them and when (ST-CA has this as an exercise, section 18.12.2). Comfort your little one before you answer any of it. Your answers can be firm or funny, as long as they aren’t mean, since mean is the Critic’s department.
The voice can also pile on. You feel sad, then call yourself pathetic for being sad, and now you’re ashamed and want to hide. You could probably have handled the sadness. The name-calling is where your Nurturer can step in.

t97b_happy_try:
How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?
What do you picture when you wish someone well? Probably them fed and safe, with people around who like them, stuff like that. Wanting that for somebody is love (babies get this part already), and practical love matters a lot. The horizon of what I can wish for someone is partly shaped by the happiness, peace, and freedom I know are possible.
But maybe you’ve had a big spiritual experience, and for a while you felt a peace or a love you didn’t know existed. After that, “I want you to be happy” can mean something much bigger, almost overnight. That’s why loving-kindness meditation can sound comically simple to someone who’s never been near that, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying “may you be happy” over and over won’t zap you into profound love, but it’s one way people find that love and grow it.
If that bigger happiness makes you curious, I’d follow the curiosity and skip pretending to believe anything. Read people from a few different traditions, say a Sufi poet and a Zen teacher. And if you ever meet someone who’s happy in a way that doesn’t add up, watch how they treat people on a day when everything’s going wrong for them.
Sometimes your little one has enough care, and what’s missing is something else. A hot meal can help, and so can saying no to your boss, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn’t be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?
Curiosity can be enough here, something like “Other people say they’ve felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don’t know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?”
t97b_shallow:
When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. Say you wake up from a dream soaked in way more feeling and need than anything the session got near. Then this is probably you. A nice session that just wears off is a different thing. I’d ask what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again after your morning coffee. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, dial the practice down by doing it earlier in the day, or for less time.
t97b_related_try:
Related Clinical Work
This framework developed through the teachers and collaborators credited below and my own practice. Later revisions also compare notes with schema therapy, compassion-focused therapy, attachment repair, motivational interviewing, mentalizing, metacognitive therapy, behavioral activation, radically open DBT, emotion-focused therapy and spiritually integrated psychotherapy. I borrow particular ideas and practices from each of them, but the mix is mine, so please don’t blame them for it.
